item.description:
Jeanette Van Tassel was a 24 year old American aeronaut whose balloon ascent over Dhaka's Buriganga River in 1892 was meant to dazzle a city. Instead, it ended in her death after a rescue attempt went tragically wrong, leaving her buried in an unmarked grave in Old Dhaka. More than a century later, a researcher's chance discovery brought her remarkable story back to light.

item.title: New geopolitical equation between Bangladesh and the United States behind the scenes. [ daily-sun ]
New York's Muslims reclaim their city 25 years after 9/11 attacks. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Asad Dandia was eight when he watched the Sept 11, 2001 attacks on television at his Pakistani-immigrant parents’ home in New York.

Then came the backlash — years of Islamophobia as Americans processed attacks that had killed nearly 3,000 people.

There was anger, suspicion and worse.

At 19, Dandia experienced a police informant posing as a friend to infiltrate his family home, part of a now-disgraced surveillance effort purportedly seeking to detect extremism.

Today, though, the 33-year-old historian finds a New York transformed: one with its first Muslim mayor, public prayers in Times Square and new mosques rising across the city.

“Twenty-five years after 9/11, we mourn and we grieve what happened, and at the same time, we recognise that I am not responsible for what happened,” he told AFP.

“I don’t deserve to be targeted for what happened, and I am as much of a New Yorker as anybody else in that respect,” said Dandia, who leads walking tours centred on the city’s Muslim communities.

Islamophobia surged in the United States after the 2001 attacks in which militants hijacked airliners and flew them into Manhattan’s World Trade Centre and the Pentagon outside Washington. A fourth plane crashed into a Pennsylvania field after a passenger revolt.

Muslims reported increased public assaults and harassment, and some stopped wearing visual markers such as hijabs in a bid to conceal their religion.

Meanwhile, US authorities monitored Muslims by requiring thousands of men and boys to register with the government, leading to many being deported from the country.

“Everyone was in such fear,” said Mohammed Razvi, a native Pakistani who founded the Council of Peoples Organisation non-profit to support Muslims in New York after 9/11.

“We had gunshots fired in our neighbourhood by individuals who felt that we were responsible,” he added.

Razvi said he started introducing himself as “Mo” after 9/11 to avoid the stigma he encountered when saying “Mohammad”.

“Muslims trying to live the American dream were being blamed for something they had nothing to do with or even control,” he said.

‘Terrifying’

In New York, police began surveilling hundreds of Muslims as part of their counterterrorism strategy, often targeting people without evidence of wrongdoing.

Dandia experienced this as a 19-year-old college student, when a young Bangladeshi man joined a mutual aid charity he had started.

The pair grew close: sharing meals, playing sports and even sleeping at Dandia’s home. But seven months later, the man revealed that he was an NYPD informant sent to monitor Dandia and his community.

“It was heartbreaking, but it was also terrifying,” he recalled. “My relationship with the world around me shifted underneath my feet.”

After his ordeal, Dandia and rights groups won a landmark legal settlement that restricted the NYPD from launching similar surveillance programmes and established a watchdog to monitor the force.

For Gadier Abbas, an attorney with the Council on American-Islamic Relations, the NYPD programme was the prime example of the “anti-Muslim hysteria” that followed 9/11.

But today, Abbas said, “there is a lot of hope”.

“You see American Muslims in every single walk of life, almost at every single level, and that’s a testament to the vibrancy of the community.”

‘Power’

New York will soon boast the largest mosque in the state — one of more than 100 added since 2001 in New York — while Muslims are a rising cultural and political force.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who took his oath of office on the Holy Quran, has become the new face of American leftist politics.

Still, Islamophobia persists in the city where around nine per cent of the population is Muslim.

In March, a far-right influencer organised a “Stop the Islamic Takeover of New York City” rally outside the mayor’s residence.

Meanwhile, a conservative senator has said Mamdani should be sent to Guantanamo Bay, the US detention camp best known for holding 9/11 suspects.

Some relatives of September 11 victims have called for Mamdani — an avid supporter of Palestinian rights — to skip this year’s 9/11 memorial, while other families have defended the mayor.

Dandia acknowledged Islamophobia had not disappeared, but he was optimistic about how far New York’s Muslim community has come.

“I’ve seen the growth of our institutional power, but also the recognition by other New Yorkers who are not Muslim, that we are all part of this city together,” he said.

“I think that’s really valuable because, you know, Rome was not built overnight, and it was not built by one person or one group of people. It was built by the community.”

item.title: Addressing safety in the country. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The growing circulation of illegal firearms across Bangladesh is becoming a threat that can no longer be treated as merely another law-and-order concern.
At a time when public confidence in safety is already under considerable pressure, the proliferation of guns and the rise in firearm-related killings make the need for effective state action greater than ever.
According to police records, at least 123 shooting incidents occurred across the country in the first seven months of this year, leaving more than 50 people dead. More alarming still, 1,311 weapons -- including rifles and submachine guns -- looted from police facilities during the August 2024 unrest and more than 257,000 rounds of ammunition also remain missing.
These figures should be a wake-up call. Illegal firearms are being used in political clashes, territorial disputes, drug-related conflicts, extortion, and criminal rivalries.
Ordinary citizens inevitably become vulnerable when such violence spills into public spaces, and people should not have to wonder whether a political confrontation, neighbourhood dispute, or criminal feud could suddenly put their lives at risk.
While the government's formation of a special unit to recover looted and illegal firearms is a welcome, albeit belated, step, it must be accompanied by sustained and measurable action.
Recovering the weapons already outside state control must be an urgent priority, while intelligence and law enforcement agencies need to identify and dismantle the networks bringing new firearms into the country.
Most importantly, enforcement cannot be selective. Political affiliation, criminal influence, or social standing must not determine who is investigated or prosecuted.
The public has a fundamental right to safety. The government must step up now -- not simply to respond to individual shootings, but to prevent the country from becoming increasingly accustomed to armed violence.

item.title: We are killing our rivers. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The latest survey from Bangladesh Inland Water Transport Authority (BIWTA) on water pollution in Dhaka is nothing short of shocking: 424 outlets are dumping an estimated 330 tons of waste every single day into the Buriganga, Turag, Balu, and Shitalakkhya rivers around Dhaka.
To reduce this to mismanagement and oversight is no longer possible and must be called what it is -- environmental negligence on a staggering scale.
When a nation’s lifelines are treated as open sewers, the consequences are inevitable: Toxic water, collapsing ecosystems, public health crises, and a future that becomes harder to salvage with each passing year.
That out of the 424 identified discharge points, 244 are linked to privately owned factories and industrial establishments, tells us of the impunity enjoyed by industries in our country, where they have felt emboldened to continue polluting our rivers and affect millions of lives.
This feeble enforcement and non-existent accountability needs to be addressed with immediate effect.
Let it be reiterated: Dhaka’s rivers are dying because the authorities responsible for protecting them have failed to act. All the mandates, budgets, and legal powers mean nothing if there is no urgency to do what is right for the people of this country.
When 330 tons of waste enter the water system daily, “monitoring” and “future plans” are meaningless. Only decisive action matters.
The respected authorities must literally clean up their act. While the long term plan must include proper sewage treatment and enforcing effluent treatment requirements without exception, there is an immediate need to prosecute violators and ensure that sewer lines are not secretly connected to rivers.
Bangladesh cannot aspire to economic transformation while its rivers remain toxic drains. The numbers in this survey are a national embarrassment and must be treated as a call to action. The authorities must prove they are willing to act, not just talk.

item.title: The next green revolution. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Bangladesh is entering one of the most critical periods in its agricultural history. Over the last five decades, the country achieved remarkable success in food production through irrigation expansion, high-yielding varieties, fertilizer use, and the hard work of millions of farmers. From a food-deficit nation after independence, Bangladesh has now become one of the world’s leading rice producers.
Yet the challenges ahead are enormous.
Climate change, shrinking cultivable land, labour shortages, rising production costs, groundwater depletion, salinity intrusion, floods, and increasing pest and disease pressure are threatening future food security. To sustain production for nearly 180 million people in the coming decades, Bangladesh must embrace a new scientific revolution in agriculture.
The future of Bangladeshi agriculture will likely be driven by biotechnology, artificial intelligence (AI), drones, precision agriculture, smart irrigation, robotics, and climate-smart farming systems.
Bangladesh produced an estimated 38 million tons of rice in 2025, according to FAO forecasts, largely driven by strong Boro and Aman harvests. However, cultivable land continues to shrink every year because of urbanization, industrialization, river erosion, and infrastructure expansion. According to the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics, farmland has been declining at around 0.19% annually.
Biotechnology and gene-edited crops
One of the biggest breakthroughs for Bangladesh may come through advanced genetics and biotechnology.
Bangladeshi agriculture already suffers from:
Traditional breeding methods are often too slow to respond to rapidly changing climate conditions.
Modern technologies such as CRISPR gene editing can now develop:
For example, ultra-short-duration rice could help haor farmers harvest before flash floods arrive, while salt-tolerant varieties could revive agriculture in coastal regions increasingly affected by sea-level rise.
Climate threat is already visible
Recently, severe flooding in northeastern Bangladesh damaged more than 46,000 hectares of standing Boro rice, threatening losses exceeding 200,000 metric tons.
Precision agriculture and artificial intelligence

Precision agriculture uses:

Research shows precision agriculture can significantly improve productivity.

Satellite technology combined with AI can revolutionize national agricultural planning.
Bangladesh can use satellite systems to:
Recent AI-based satellite mapping studies in Bangladesh have shown remarkable accuracy in identifying erosion-prone farmland and disappearing settlements.
Future outlook: Bangladesh 2035
If Bangladesh aggressively adopts modern agricultural technologies over the next decade, the transformation could be dramatic.

The way forward
Technology alone will not solve Bangladesh’s agricultural challenges. The country must also:
Bangladesh once achieved a historic Green Revolution through irrigation, improved seeds, and farmer resilience. The next revolution will likely come through science, artificial intelligence, biotechnology, precision farming, drones, robotics, and climate-smart innovation.
The countries that dominate future agriculture will not necessarily have the most land -- they will have the smartest farming systems.
Bangladesh now has an opportunity to become not only food-secure, but also a global example of climate-resilient scientific agriculture.

item.title: If nothing changes, then nothing changes. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
This past week, a city neighbourhood witnessed a violent turf war for control of the illicit drug trade. Several people sustained gunshot wounds, though, fortunately, no one was killed.
An initial probe found politically-linked drug dealers behind the violence, with the clashes apparently driven entirely by the desire to secure territory under a new political settlement.
Only a couple of weeks ago, this paper ran a report detailing how trucks carrying fruit to the city’s prime trading hub were caught in a web of extortion. Truck drivers at Dhaka’s Badamtoli riverfront wholesale fruit market face systematic extortion by an illegal syndicate that uses government-authorized parking arrangements as a front.
Operators are charged more than 20 times the official parking fee simply to access the area, with a local ruling-party leader accused of directing the unauthorized collections.
Meanwhile, Shahed Sharif, a teenager, created a website named “ghush.site” late last month to protest the constant demands for bribes he faced while trying to withdraw his late schoolteacher mother’s pension.
Numerous citizens have since shared their own grievances on the platform. Up until the afternoon of September 1, a total of 11,666 complaints had been submitted to Shahed’s bribe-tracking site, with the total amount demanded reaching more than Tk357 crore.
In addition, recent surprise visits by high-ranking government officials to hospitals and land offices have revealed the dismal state of public services, with too many staff members remaining willfully absent.
All these examples speak poorly of the state of affairs in post-Monsoon Revolution Bangladesh. Aspirations were high -- not only to get rid of an authoritarian regime but also to witness a qualitative change in the country. Yet, if nothing changes, then nothing changes.
Though currently in a very difficult position, citizens can still endure the energy crisis if they receive a credible assurance from the government that efforts are underway to provide respite from gas shortages and electricity load-shedding.
These are not systemic failures per se; they can be addressed with the right steps. But when it comes to the quality of public life, certain things matter far more.
If your neighbourhood is not yet safe for your sons and daughters to move around in, and if dens of drug dealers remain operational, what change are we talking about?
If fruit vendors charge you more for every apple you buy on the “genuine” excuse that political elements have inflated prices through illicit extortion, what change are we talking about?
If institution after institution remains infested with bribery rackets, what public services can citizens expect from a “changed Bangladesh?”
In some recent heinous crime cases, law enforcers managed to apprehend the “criminals” very promptly. But when public suspicion runs high over the authenticity of those “captures,” it speaks volumes about the growing distrust of state institutions.
This is not a sign of a healthy democracy. It is a testament to the fact that, long after the changeover, we still have not managed to rebuild institutions that have long lacked transparency and accountability.
One no longer needs Transparency International or other social barometers to publish annual corruption reports on Bangladesh; citizens are literally living through graft in their daily lives.
Shahed Sharif’s website is just one glaring example of how corruption has become all-pervasive in a society where public offices are not yet held accountable.
At the level of state governance, it is well understood that until an aggressive catalyst alters legislative, electoral, or structural inputs, systemic inertia keeps public policies, economic trajectories, and institutional cultures stagnant.
Regime change by default does not make a substantive difference unless the political leadership embodies that change.
Over the years, the political system has been structured in a way that blurs the line between the government and the ruling party.
Power elites quickly become preoccupied with appeasing a large number of beneficiaries who manage to secure positions on one party front or another.
Consequently, undue advantages in work contracts, illicit toll collections, and the drug trade become inherent to the system.
With every change of guard, one group of politicians and their sidekicks simply replaces the old beneficiaries, while ordinary people -- the main stakeholders -- are forced to take a back seat.
As a result, citizens rarely see a tangible difference in their everyday lives. They still have to navigate the open trade of illicit drugs in their neighbourhoods, unsafe roads, illegal tolls in marketplaces, and bribery for every service they are entitled to as citizens of Bangladesh.
Governments often become trapped in cycles of compounding stagnation and the status quo because their primary motivation is catering to a narrow constituency: Party leaders and cadres.
In the process, they become oblivious to the everyday challenges faced by the wider population in a democracy.
When institutions remain weak and public offices fail to provide due services, entrenched special interest groups, lobbyists, and party cadres optimize their profits from the entire state system.
Reaz Ahmad is Editor, Dhaka Tribune.

item.title: Reeling in reels. [ newagebd ]
item.description: SHORT videos dubbed as reels are engaging millions of people, especially the young generation, every moment. It is dopamine and algorithms behind the reels that are at play to snatch away time from them. People are drawn into the hook by easy, immediate rewards of self-gratification and the more they are so, the hungrier they become to make life increasingly thrilled and ultra-motivated. Routine life — reading, resting, pausing for some time to ponder, meeting people or sitting cosily at the twilight in the living room and sipping tea with the family — feel like biting some stale bread to them...

item.title: Gas beneath feet and billions we chose to import. [ newagebd ]
item.description: BANGLADESH has spent years looking for gas in wrong places, not necessarily geographically, but politically. While the country has increasingly turned to expensive imported liquefied natural gas to keep industries, power plants and fertiliser factories running, a substantial domestic gas resource has remained stranded in Bhola. The irony is difficult to ignore: the country did not simply fail to find an alternative to imported energy. It appears to have postponed an alternative that was already known to exist...
